subChunks.title: Generic Classes & Type Parameters
subChunks.hookHtml:
You write a Box class to hold a String. Then you need one for Integer. Then for Spell. You end up copy-pasting the same logic three times, swapping only the type name. Somewhere, a compiler weeps.

Generics let you write one class that works safely with any type — no duplication, no casting, no ClassCastException landmines at runtime.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's Grand Library held a peculiar archive: shelf after shelf of identical wooden boxes, each labelled with a different rune — 'String Box', 'Integer Box', 'Spell Box', 'Dragon Box'. The apprentice stared at the absurdity.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Observe the futility. Every box works identically — put something in, take it out. Yet we maintain a separate class for each type. If I added a new type tomorrow, someone would have to carve another box.

storyBeats.speaker: Apprentice
storyBeats.text: Why not just store everything as an Object?

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Because then you lose all type information. You put in a String, you get back an Object. You must cast it — and if you cast it wrong, you get a ClassCastException at runtime. The compiler cannot warn you. Bugs hide until production.

storyBeats.label: The Object approach — compiles, explodes at runtime

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Generics solve this with a type parameter — a placeholder declared with angle brackets. Write Box<T> and the compiler treats T as a stand-in for whatever type the caller specifies. Type safety is enforced at compile time, not runtime.

storyBeats.label: Generic Box — one class, infinite types, zero casts

storyBeats.text: The shelves of duplicate boxes vanished, replaced by a single elegant template etched in silver. The apprentice noticed the diamond operator — <> — on the right side of the declaration.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The diamond operator on the right-hand side tells the compiler: infer the type from the left. You do not need to write new Box<String>() — new Box<>() suffices. Convention uses single uppercase letters: T for Type, E for Element, K and V for Key and Value.

storyBeats.label: Multiple type parameters — a generic Pair

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Note that you cannot use primitive types as type arguments. Write Box<int> and the compiler refuses. Use wrapper classes — Integer, Double, Boolean. Java's autoboxing handles the conversion silently when assigning literals.

subChunks.explanationHtml:
Generic Classes

A generic class declares one or more type parameters in angle brackets after the class name:

class Box<T> { ... }

T is a placeholder. Every use of T inside the class is replaced by the actual type when a caller instantiates Box<String> or Box<Integer>.

Why generics?

  • Type safety: the compiler rejects wrong-type assignments at compile time, not runtime.
  • No casting: box.get() returns exactly T, not Object — no cast required.
  • DRY: one class, all types.

Type parameter conventions

LetterMeaningExample
TType (generic)Box<T>
EElementList<E>
K, VKey, ValueMap<K, V>
RReturn typeFunction results

Diamond operator

On the right side of a declaration, <> tells the compiler to infer the type from the variable declaration:

Box<String> box = new Box<>(); // infers Box<String>

Primitives not allowed

Type parameters must be reference types. Use wrapper classes: Integer, Double, Boolean, Character. Autoboxing converts primitives automatically when assigning literals.

Multiple type parameters

class Pair<K, V> {
    K key;
    V value;
    Pair(K k, V v) { key = k; value = v; }
}
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Task: Build a Generic Result<T> class

In many APIs, an operation either succeeds (returning a value) or fails (returning an error message). Model this as a generic class:

  • Fields: private T value, private String error, private boolean success
  • Two static factory methods: ok(T value) sets success=true and stores the value; fail(String error) sets success=false and stores the error message
  • boolean isSuccess() — returns success
  • T getValue() — returns value (may be null if failed)
  • String getError() — returns error (may be null if succeeded)
  • toString() — returns "OK: " + value when successful, "FAIL: " + error when not

The main method is already written — your job is to complete the class so its output matches exactly.

guidedPracticeTests.label: ok() result prints 'OK: Fireball cast!'
guidedPracticeTests.expected:
OK: Fireball cast!
FAIL: Not enough mana
true
50

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Solo Challenge: Generic Stack

Implement a Stack<T> class backed by an ArrayList:

  • void push(T item) — adds item to the top
  • T pop() — removes and returns the top item; if empty, prints Stack is empty and returns null
  • T peek() — returns the top item without removing it; if empty, returns null
  • boolean isEmpty() — returns true if no items
  • int size() — returns item count
  • toString() — returns [bottom, ..., top] format

Test with a Stack<String> pushing three spells, peeking, popping all, then attempting a pop on the empty stack.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a non-programmer why Java generics exist. Use an analogy — perhaps a filing cabinet that only accepts specific types of documents. Why is a generic filing cabinet better than one that accepts 'anything' but loses track of what's inside?

questions.questionHtml: What does the T in class Box<T> represent?
options: A type parameter — a placeholder for any reference type specified when creating a Box
The letter T specifically — Box can only hold types whose name starts with T
A template keyword similar to C++
An interface that all stored values must implement
questions.correctAnswer: A type parameter — a placeholder for any reference type specified when creating a Box
questions.explanationHtml: T is a type parameter — a placeholder resolved when the caller writes Box<String> or Box<Integer>. It can be any reference type.

questions.questionHtml: Box<int> b = new Box<>(); is valid Java.
questions.explanationHtml: Type parameters must be reference types, not primitives. Use the wrapper class Integer instead: Box<Integer>.

questions.questionHtml: Given class Pair<K, V>, which instantiation correctly creates a pair mapping a String key to an Integer value?
options: Pair<String, Integer> p = new Pair<>("key", 42);
Pair p = new Pair("key", 42);
Pair<K, V> p = new Pair<>("key", 42);
Pair<String> p = new Pair<>("key", 42);
questions.explanationHtml: Both type arguments must be supplied: Pair<String, Integer>. The diamond operator on the right infers from the left. Raw types (no angle brackets) lose type safety.

questions.questionHtml: What is the key difference between Box<Object> and Box<T> (a generic class)?
options: Box<Object> accepts any type but loses type information at extraction — a cast is required and can fail at runtime. Box<T> preserves the exact type so the compiler enforces correct usage.
Box<Object> and Box<T> are identical — generics are just syntactic sugar for Object.
Box<T> is slower because generics require reflection at runtime.
Box<Object> is only usable with String and Integer; Box<T> works with all types.
questions.correctAnswer: Box<Object> accepts any type but loses type information at extraction — a cast is required and can fail at runtime. Box<T> preserves the exact type so the compiler enforces correct usage.
questions.explanationHtml: Box<Object>.get() returns Object — you must cast it, and a wrong cast silently compiles but crashes at runtime. With Box<T>, get() returns exactly T; wrong types are rejected at compile time.

subChunks.title: Generic Methods & Bounded Types
subChunks.hookHtml:
Your generic Box<T> works for any type — but what if you need to compare what's inside? Or call .length() on it? With a plain T, the compiler refuses: it has no idea what type T actually is.

Bounded type parameters let you constrain T — 'any type, but it must implement Comparable'. Suddenly, your generic code can call methods, and the compiler still has your back.

storyBeats.text: Having mastered the generic Box, the apprentice grew ambitious. She wanted to write a method that found the larger of two values — but her generic method wouldn't compile. The compiler refused to call compareTo on a plain T.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The issue is this: when you write T with no constraints, the compiler assumes it could be anything — including a type with no useful methods at all. You must declare a bound: T extends Comparable<T> tells the compiler that whatever T is, it guarantees the compareTo method.

storyBeats.label: Bounded type parameter — finds the maximum

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Notice that the bound uses extends even for interfaces — T extends Comparable<T>, not implements. This is Java's convention for bounds. You may bound with multiple types using &: T extends Comparable<T> & Serializable.
The apprentice noticed the static <T> before the return type — different from the class-level parameter.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Good eye. A generic method declares its own type parameter independently, even inside a generic class. The <T> before the return type is mandatory — it introduces T for that method alone. The method's T is resolved per call, not per class instantiation.

storyBeats.label: Generic method in a non-generic class

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: One final pattern: type erasure. At compile time, generics are checked thoroughly. At runtime, the JVM erases the type parameter — Box<String> and Box<Integer> are the same Box at runtime. This is why you cannot write new T() or instanceof Box<String>. Generics are a compile-time safety net, not a runtime mechanism.

storyBeats.label: Type erasure — what the JVM actually sees

subChunks.explanationHtml:
Generic Methods

Any method — static or instance, inside a generic class or not — can declare its own type parameters. The syntax puts <T> before the return type:

public static <T> T identity(T value) {
    return value;
}

Each call site resolves T independently based on the argument type.

Bounded Type Parameters

A plain T provides no methods beyond those on Object. To call specific methods, add an upper bound with extends:

// T must implement Comparable<T>
public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(T a, T b) {
    return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
}

Now compareTo is available on every T. The bound can be a class or an interface; the keyword is always extends in this context.

Multiple bounds

// T must be a Number AND implement Comparable
<T extends Number & Comparable<T>>

A class bound (if any) must come first; interface bounds follow with &.

Type Erasure

Generics are a compile-time feature. The JVM erases type parameters at runtime — Box<String> becomes raw Box. Consequences:

  • Cannot create instances of type parameters: new T() is illegal
  • Cannot use instanceof with generic types: obj instanceof List<String> is illegal
  • Can use raw type checks: obj instanceof List is fine

Wildcards (preview)

You may see List<?> — an unbounded wildcard meaning 'a List of some unknown type'. Wildcards are used in method parameters to accept wider ranges of generic types. They are read-only for the unknown type; you can call size() and get() but not add(). Full wildcard rules are an Advanced topic.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Task: Generic MinMax<T> Tracker

Build a class that tracks the minimum and maximum values seen so far among any Comparable type:

  • Class signature: class MinMax<T extends Comparable<T>>
  • void add(T value) — updates min and max if needed; initialises both on the first call
  • T getMin() — returns the minimum seen (or null if empty)
  • T getMax() — returns the maximum seen (or null if empty)
  • toString() — returns "min=X max=Y"

The main method tests it with integers and strings — make it pass.

guidedPracticeTests.label: MinMax tracks min and max correctly for integers and strings

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Solo Challenge: Generic Cache<K, V>

Build a simple fixed-capacity generic cache:

  • Constructor takes a int capacity
  • void put(K key, V value) — stores the value; if already at capacity, print Cache full and do nothing
  • V get(K key) — returns the value for the key, or null if not present
  • boolean containsKey(K key)
  • int size()
  • toString() — returns the underlying map's toString

Backed by a HashMap<K, V> internally. Test with a Cache<String, Integer> of capacity 2.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain type erasure to someone who knows what generics are but is confused about why you cannot write 'new T()' or check 'instanceof List<String>'. Use an analogy of a shipping label that gets removed once the package is en route — the warehouse can read it, but the delivery truck cannot.

questions.questionHtml: What does <T extends Comparable<T>> mean on a method?
options: T must be a type that implements the Comparable interface, allowing compareTo to be called inside the method
T must extend the Comparable class directly using class inheritance
T can be any type; the bound is just documentation and not enforced
T is limited to numeric types (Integer, Double, Long)
questions.correctAnswer: T must be a type that implements the Comparable interface, allowing compareTo to be called inside the method
questions.explanationHtml: The extends keyword in a type bound can mean 'implements' for interfaces. T extends Comparable<T> means T must implement Comparable, guaranteeing compareTo is available.

questions.questionHtml: After compilation, Box<String> and Box<Integer> are different classes at runtime.
questions.explanationHtml: Type erasure removes generic type information at compile time. At runtime, both are simply Box — the JVM has no notion of Box<String> vs Box<Integer>.

options: <T extends Comparable<T>>
<T>
<T implements Comparable<T>>
Comparable
questions.explanationHtml: <T extends Comparable<T>> is required so the compiler knows compareTo is available on T. Plain <T> would prevent the compareTo call. 'implements' is not valid syntax for type bounds.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is NOT allowed due to type erasure?
options: if (list instanceof List<String>) { ... }
List<String> words = new ArrayList<>();
if (list instanceof List) { ... }
T value = box.getValue();
questions.explanationHtml: Checking instanceof with a parameterised type like List<String> is illegal because the JVM has erased the String parameter — it can only see List. Raw type instanceof (option 3) is fine. The other options are standard generic usage.
